chapitres.resume: Axe 1, Identités et échanges : l'immigration au Canada, la Windrush generation au Royaume-Uni, la frontière irlandaise. Grammaire : choisir un temps du passé, le past perfect, les marqueurs temporels, used to / would et le futur dans le passé.
chapitres.chapeau: Millions of people have left their country to start a new life in Canada, in Britain or elsewhere. Their arrival changed their new homes, and their new homes changed them. Borders can separate people, but they can also be places where identities meet. Dans ce chapitre, tu lis trois histoires de migrations et de frontières, et tu apprends à raconter un parcours au passé en situant précisément les événements les uns par rapport aux autres.
objectifs: présenter la politique d'immigration du Canada, de Pier 21 au multiculturalisme ;
raconter l'histoire de la Windrush generation et expliquer le scandale de 2018 ;
expliquer pourquoi la frontière entre l'Irlande et l'Irlande du Nord est un enjeu d'identité ;
employer le vocabulaire des migrations, de la citoyenneté et de l'identité ;
choisir entre prétérit simple, prétérit be + -ing et present perfect ;
exprimer l'antériorité dans le passé avec le past perfect ;
situer des événements avec des marqueurs temporels, used to, would et le futur dans le passé.

sections.html:
Le Canada se présente souvent comme un pays d'accueil. Lis le texte et repère trois étapes de sa politique d'immigration, puis ses zones d'ombre.

Pier 21

Between 1928 and 1971, about one million immigrants arrived in Canada through Pier 21, in the port of Halifax, Nova Scotia. After a long voyage across the Atlantic, they showed their papers, had a medical check and took a train to their new life. Today the building is the Canadian Museum of Immigration.

From origin to skills

For a long time, Canada chose its immigrants according to their country of origin and preferred Europeans. In 1967, the government introduced a points system: candidates now received points for their education, their knowledge of English or French and their work experience, not for their nationality. Skilled workers from Asia, Africa and the Caribbean could now be eligible.

In 1971, Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau announced a policy of multiculturalism: newcomers did not have to give up their culture to become Canadian. Canada was the first country in the world to adopt such a policy, and the Canadian Multiculturalism Act followed in 1988.

Canada today

According to the 2021 census, almost one Canadian in four (23 %) is or has been an immigrant. Newcomers arrive as skilled workers, through family sponsorship (a relative who already lives in Canada supports their application) or as refugees. Since 1979, groups of ordinary citizens have also been able to sponsor refugees privately: between November 2015 and February 2016, Canada welcomed more than 25,000 Syrian refugees.

A darker past

This open image has its shadows. From 1885, Chinese immigrants had to pay a head tax to enter the country, and a law excluded almost all of them from 1923 to 1947. In 1914, the ship Komagata Maru, carrying 376 passengers, most of them Sikhs from India, was turned away from Vancouver. The Canadian government apologised for the head tax in 2006 and for the Komagata Maru in 2016.

Méthode

Pour résumer un texte historique, relève les dates et associe chacune à un changement : 1967 → points system, 1971 → multiculturalism. Une frise chronologique (timeline) t'aide à restituer l'ordre des événements à l'oral.

En 1948, un navire arrive des Caraïbes en Angleterre. Ses passagers donnent leur nom à toute une génération. Lis le texte et repère ce que ces migrants ont apporté au Royaume-Uni, et comment ils ont été traités.

22 June 1948

On 22 June 1948, the ship HMT Empire Windrush arrived at Tilbury Docks, near London. On board were more than a thousand passengers, most of them from Jamaica, Trinidad and other Caribbean islands, which were British colonies at the time. Among them was the calypso singer Lord Kitchener, who sang London Is the Place for Me for the cameras.

That same year, the British Nationality Act made people from the colonies "citizens of the United Kingdom and Colonies": they had the right to live and work in Britain. The country needed them. After the Second World War, Britain had to rebuild its cities, and the new National Health Service (NHS), London Transport and the railways were looking for workers.

A lasting contribution

The people who came from the Caribbean between 1948 and 1971 are known as the Windrush generation. They worked as nurses, bus drivers, factory workers and engineers. Their culture changed British society: calypso, reggae, Caribbean food, and the Notting Hill Carnival, which has been held in London every August since 1966.

Life was not easy. Many landlords put up signs saying "No Irish, no Blacks, no dogs", and in 1958 white gangs attacked Caribbean residents during the Notting Hill riots. Yet the newcomers stayed, built communities and became part of the nation. One of the passengers, Sam King, became the first Black mayor of the London borough of Southwark in 1983.

The Windrush scandal

In 2018, the public discovered that hundreds of people from the Windrush generation had been wrongly treated as illegal immigrants. They had arrived legally as children, but they had never needed papers to prove it. The Home Office had even destroyed their landing cards in 2010. Some lost their jobs or their homes, some were refused healthcare, and some were sent to detention centres or deported. The Home Secretary, Amber Rudd, resigned, and the government created a compensation scheme. Since 2018, Windrush Day has celebrated the contribution of Caribbean migrants every year on 22 June.

L'île d'Irlande est partagée entre deux États. Lis le texte et repère comment cette frontière a d'abord séparé, puis rapproché, les habitants de l'île.

One island, two states

In 1921, Ireland was divided. Twenty-six counties became the Irish Free State, which later became the Republic of Ireland, while six counties in the north-east remained part of the United Kingdom as Northern Ireland. The border between them is about 500 kilometres long and crosses fields, villages and even farms.

In Northern Ireland, two communities lived side by side. Most unionists, mainly Protestants, wanted to stay British. Most nationalists, mainly Catholics, wished to join the Republic. Even the name of the second city depends on who you are talking to: Derry for many nationalists, Londonderry for many unionists.

The Troubles

From the late 1960s to 1998, a violent conflict known as the Troubles killed more than 3,500 people. During those years, the border was guarded by soldiers, with armed checkpoints and watchtowers, and many small roads were closed.

Peace and an open border

On 10 April 1998, the Good Friday Agreement brought peace. It recognised that the people of Northern Ireland may identify as British, Irish or both, and hold a British passport, an Irish passport or both. The checkpoints disappeared, and today you can cross the border without noticing it: people go to school, work or shop on the other side every day.

After Brexit

When the United Kingdom left the European Union in 2020, the open border became a problem, because it was now a border between the EU and a non-EU country. To avoid a "hard border" with checkpoints, London and Brussels agreed to carry out checks on some goods travelling between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, in the Irish Sea; the Windsor Framework of 2023 adjusted this arrangement. In Belfast, some "peace walls" still separate the two communities: the border question is also a question of identity.

Définition

Une frontière dure (hard border) comporte des postes de contrôle physiques ; une frontière ouverte (open border) se franchit librement. Le Royaume-Uni et l'Irlande forment depuis 1923 une zone de libre circulation, la Common Travel Area.

Faux amis

To pretend = faire semblant (prétendre = to claim). Actually = en fait (actuellement = currently, nowadays). A deception = une tromperie (une déception = a disappointment).

Pour raconter un parcours, il faut choisir le bon temps. Le choix dépend de la manière dont tu regardes l'action, pas seulement de sa date.

Le prétérit simple : une action terminée, datée

Il présente un fait passé, coupé du présent, souvent avec un repère daté (in 1948, ago, last year, when) : The Windrush arrived in 1948. Trudeau announced the policy in 1971.

Verbes irréguliers fréquents : come → came, leave → left, bring → brought, take → took, become → became, build → built, give → gave, lose → lost, choose → chose, send → sent.

Le prétérit be + -ing : une action en cours dans le passé

Il décrit une action en déroulement à un moment passé, souvent interrompue par une action au prétérit simple : The passengers were waiting on the deck when the ship arrived. Il sert aussi à poser un décor : It was raining and people were cheering.

When introduit souvent l'action courte (prétérit simple), while l'action longue (be + -ing) : While she was working at the hospital, she met her husband.

Le present perfect : un lien entre passé et présent

Il s'emploie quand le passé a un lien avec le présent : un bilan, une conséquence, une durée qui continue. On ne peut pas l'employer avec un repère daté et terminé.

  • bilan : Canada has welcomed millions of immigrants.
  • durée jusqu'à maintenant avec for (durée) et since (point de départ) : The carnival has been held since 1966. She has lived in Toronto for ten years.
  • avec already, ever, never, yet, just : Have you ever been to Halifax?
PhraseTempsPourquoi
She came to London in 1956.prétérit simpledate passée terminée
She has lived in London since 1956.present perfectelle y vit toujours
She was living in London when she met him.prétérit be + -ingaction en cours, interrompue
Attention

« Elle vit à Londres depuis 1956 » se dit She has lived in London since 1956 et non She lives in London since 1956. Et « il est arrivé il y a dix ans » se dit He arrived ten years ago (prétérit, jamais de present perfect avec ago).

Forme

had + participe passé, à toutes les personnes : I had left, she had arrived, they had never needed. Négation : had not (hadn't) + participe passé. Question : Had they arrived?

Emploi : le passé du passé

Le past perfect exprime une action antérieure à un autre moment du passé. Il correspond souvent au plus-que-parfait français (« ils étaient arrivés »).

  • In 2018, they discovered that the Home Office had destroyed the landing cards. (la destruction a eu lieu avant la découverte)
  • When the ship docked, the passengers had already spent three weeks at sea.
  • By the time the Troubles ended, more than 3,500 people had died.

Compare :

  • When I arrived, the train left. : j'arrive, puis le train part (succession).
  • When I arrived, the train had left. : le train était déjà parti (antériorité).

Les repères qui l'accompagnent souvent

already, just, never… before, by the time, after, before, when, until : She had never seen snow before she landed in Halifax.

Le past perfect be + -ing

had been + V-ing insiste sur la durée d'une activité jusqu'à un moment passé : They had been living in Britain for fifty years when they were told to leave.

Attention

On n'emploie pas le past perfect quand l'ordre des actions est évident et suit l'ordre du récit : She got off the ship, took a train and found a room. Le past perfect sert à revenir en arrière dans le temps.

sections.titre: Grammar: time markers, used to, would, was going to
sections.html:
Situer dans le temps

RelationMarqueursExemple
antérioritébefore, by the time, until, earlierBy the time she retired, she had worked for the NHS for 40 years.
simultanéitéwhile, as, when, in the meantime, meanwhileWhile the soldiers watched the border, smugglers used small roads.
postérioritéafter, as soon as, once, afterwards, later, the following yearAs soon as the ship docked, journalists rushed on board.
duréefor, since, over the past years, during, in a couple of daysOver the past years, immigration has increased.

Après when, as soon as, once, until, before, after à valeur future, on emploie le présent (et non will) : I'll call you as soon as I arrive.

L'habitude dans le passé : used to et would

  • used to + BV : une habitude ou un état passé qui n'existe plus : Soldiers used to check every car. There used to be a watchtower here. Négation : didn't use to ; question : Did you use to…?
  • would + BV : une action répétée dans le passé, souvent dans un récit de souvenirs : Every Sunday, my grandmother would cook rice and peas. Would ne s'emploie pas pour un état : She used to live in Kingston (pas would live).
Ne confonds pas

I used to work at night (j'avais l'habitude, ce n'est plus le cas) ; I am used to working at night (je suis habitué à) ; I got used to working at night (je me suis habitué à). Après be used to et get used to, to est une préposition : on emploie V-ing.

Le futur dans le passé

Pour parler, dans un récit au passé, de ce qui était alors à venir :

  • was / were going to + BV : une intention passée, souvent non réalisée : Many passengers were going to stay for five years, but they never went back.
  • would + BV : ce qui allait arriver, vu depuis le passé : In 1948, nobody knew that the ship would give its name to a generation.

chapitres.a_retenir:
• Le Canada a ouvert son immigration avec le système à points (1967) et la politique du multiculturalisme (1971) ; près d'un Canadien sur quatre est immigré (recensement de 2021). Son passé comporte aussi des exclusions (taxe d'entrée imposée aux Chinois, Komagata Maru).
  • La Windrush generation désigne les migrants venus des Caraïbes entre 1948 et 1971 pour aider à reconstruire le Royaume-Uni ; en 2018, le Windrush scandal a révélé que beaucoup avaient été traités à tort comme des clandestins.
  • La frontière irlandaise date de 1921 ; l'accord du Vendredi saint (1998) a mis fin aux Troubles et permet d'être britannique, irlandais ou les deux. Le Brexit a reposé la question de la frontière.
  • Prétérit simple : fait daté et terminé. Prétérit be + -ing : action en cours dans le passé. Present perfect : lien avec le présent (bilan, for, since), jamais avec ago ni une date terminée.
  • Past perfect (had + participe passé) : action antérieure à un autre moment du passé.
  • used to + BV : habitude ou état passé révolu ; would + BV : action répétée dans un souvenir ; was going to / would : futur vu depuis le passé.

chapitres.resume: Axe 2, Diversité et inclusion : logement et mixité sociale, la Cour suprême des États-Unis, la représentation politique des Peuples premiers. Grammaire : la voix passive, les propositions relatives (who, whom, whose, which, that), want / expect sb to.
chapitres.chapeau: Who can live where? Who decides what is fair? Who speaks for minorities? In the English-speaking world, laws, courts and parliaments have sometimes excluded minorities and sometimes opened the door to them. Dans ce chapitre, tu étudies le logement, la Cour suprême américaine et la place des Peuples premiers en politique, et tu apprends à présenter une décision au passif, à relier des informations avec des relatives et à exprimer ce que l'on attend des autres.
objectifs: expliquer comment les politiques du logement ont pu renforcer ou combattre la ségrégation ;
présenter le rôle de la Cour suprême des États-Unis et quelques grands arrêts ;
décrire des formes de représentation politique des Peuples premiers et le débat qu'elles suscitent ;
employer le vocabulaire de la discrimination, de la justice et de l'inclusion ;
former et employer la voix passive à tous les temps ;
relier des idées avec les pronoms relatifs, dont whose et whom ;
exprimer une volonté ou une attente avec want, expect, would like + sb + to.

sections.titre: Where you live, who you are?
sections.html:
Le lieu où l'on vit détermine l'accès à l'école, à l'emploi, aux transports. Lis le texte et repère comment des politiques publiques ont favorisé la ségrégation, puis tenté de la combattre.

Redlining in the United States

In the 1930s, during the Great Depression, a federal agency, the Home Owners' Loan Corporation, drew maps of American cities. Each neighbourhood received a grade from A to D. The "hazardous" D areas were coloured in red, and they were very often the neighbourhoods where Black families and immigrants lived. Banks then refused to lend money to people in those areas, or charged them more. This practice is called redlining.

Redlining denied millions of families access to homeownership, the main way to build wealth in the United States. It was banned by the Fair Housing Act, signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson in April 1968, a week after the assassination of Martin Luther King. Yet its effects can still be seen today: many formerly redlined neighbourhoods have higher poverty rates and fewer trees and parks.

Gated communities

Today, some wealthy Americans live in gated communities, residential areas surrounded by walls, with guards at the entrance. Residents say they feel safer; critics say these areas separate "the haves and the have-nots" and weaken the sense of a shared city.

Social housing in Britain

In the United Kingdom, local councils built millions of council houses after the Second World War, so that working families could rent a decent home. From 1980, the Right to Buy allowed tenants to buy their council homes, but few new ones were built. Today, many cities try to build mixed-tenure neighbourhoods, where private homes and social housing stand side by side. The fire at Grenfell Tower, a social housing block in one of the richest areas of London, killed 72 people in June 2017 and became a symbol of the gap between rich and poor residents.

sections.titre: The Supreme Court: inclusion and exclusion
sections.html:
Aux États-Unis, la Cour suprême dit si les lois respectent la Constitution. Ses décisions ont tantôt exclu, tantôt inclus les minorités. Lis le texte et classe les arrêts cités en deux colonnes : exclusion et inclusion.

How the Court works

The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States. It is made up of nine Justices, led by the Chief Justice. They are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, and they serve for life. When a Justice dies or retires, the President can fill the vacancy, which is why each nomination is a major political battle. The Court decides by majority; a Justice who disagrees with the majority can write a dissenting opinion.

From exclusion…

In Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), the Court ruled that racial segregation was legal as long as facilities were "separate but equal". In practice, schools, trains and hospitals for Black Americans were separate, but far from equal. This decision protected segregation in the South for more than half a century.

… to inclusion

In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Court, led by Chief Justice Earl Warren, ruled unanimously that segregated public schools were unconstitutional. The lawyer who won the case, Thurgood Marshall, became the first Black Justice in 1967. Other decisions followed: Loving v. Virginia (1967) allowed interracial marriage in every state, and Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) did the same for same-sex marriage.

A court that can change its mind

The Court can also overturn its own precedents. In 2022, it overturned Roe v. Wade (1973), which had protected the right to abortion: each state can now decide. In 2023, it ruled that universities could no longer take race into account in their admissions, ending the use of affirmative action in college admissions. For some, these decisions protect the Constitution; for others, they wipe out rights that minorities had won.

Des juges qui ont marqué l'histoire

Ruth Bader Ginsburg, deuxième femme nommée à la Cour (1993-2020), célèbre pour ses opinions dissidentes ; Sonia Sotomayor, première juge d'origine hispanique (2009) ; Ketanji Brown Jackson, première femme noire (2022).

Comment les Peuples premiers (First Peoples, Indigenous peoples) peuvent-ils faire entendre leur voix dans les institutions ? Lis le texte et compare deux réponses, en Nouvelle-Zélande et en Australie.

New Zealand: Māori seats

In 1840, the British Crown and more than 500 Māori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi, which is considered the founding document of New Zealand. In 1867, Parliament created four Māori seats, elected only by Māori voters, and gave the vote to all Māori men. There are now seven Māori electorates, and Māori MPs also sit for ordinary constituencies. Te reo Māori has been an official language since 1987.

Australia: the Voice referendum

In Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples were long excluded. In the 1967 referendum, more than 90 % of voters agreed that they should be counted in the national census and that the federal government could make laws for them. In 2023, Australians were asked whether an Indigenous Voice to Parliament, an advisory body, should be written into the Constitution. On 14 October 2023, about 60 % voted no, and the proposal was rejected in every state.

Integration or appropriation?

Reserved seats and advisory bodies divide opinion. Supporters say they guarantee that First Peoples are heard and help to right historical wrongs. Critics answer that they can be symbolic only, giving recognition without real power, or that the majority uses Indigenous culture and symbols without sharing decisions. Others, on the contrary, reject any separate representation in the name of equality.

In the United States, Native Americans became citizens of the country in 1924. In 2021, Deb Haaland, a member of the Laguna Pueblo, became the first Native American to serve as a cabinet secretary.

Méthode : nuancer son accord

I partly agree with this idea, but… / That's a valid point; however… / I see what you mean, yet I differ from you on… / Let's agree to disagree.

Ces listes reprennent le lexique du programme (discrimination et exclusion ; la Cour suprême ; mobilité sociale).

Discrimination and exclusion

The Supreme Court

Social mobility

EnglishFrançaisExample

to ensure equal opportunitiesgarantir l'égalité des chancesLaws must ensure equal opportunities.

Forme

be (au temps voulu) + participe passé. C'est be qui porte le temps ; le complément d'agent est introduit par by.

TempsActifPassif
présent simpleThe Senate confirms the Justices.The Justices are confirmed by the Senate.
présent be + -ingThey are building new homes.New homes are being built.
prétéritThe Court overturned Roe v. Wade.Roe v. Wade was overturned.
present perfectParliament has created seven seats.Seven seats have been created.
past perfectThe agency had drawn maps.Maps had been drawn.
avec modalEach state can decide the question.The question can be decided by each state.
futurVoters will elect a new MP.A new MP will be elected.

Quand l'employer ?

  • quand l'agent est inconnu, évident ou sans importance : The Fair Housing Act was signed in 1968.
  • pour mettre en valeur ce qui subit l'action : Thousands of families were denied loans.
  • dans les textes officiels, juridiques et journalistiques.

Le passif des verbes à deux compléments

Avec give, offer, grant, tell, deny, la personne devient souvent le sujet : They gave Māori men the vote. → Māori men were given the vote. C'est l'équivalent de « on » en français : On leur a refusé un prêt = They were refused a loan.

Be said to, be thought to

He is said to be the best lawyer in the state : on dit qu'il est… The Treaty is considered (to be) the founding document of New Zealand.

Attention

Les verbes intransitifs (arrive, happen, die) n'ont pas de passif. Et le « on » français ne se traduit pas toujours par le passif : On dit que… = People say that… ou It is said that…

Une proposition relative apporte une information sur un nom (l'antécédent). Le pronom relatif dépend de l'antécédent et de sa fonction.

PronomAntécédentExemple
whopersonne, sujet (ou complément à l'oral)the lawyer who won the case
whompersonne, complément (registre soutenu), après prépositionthe Justice whom the President nominated / the chiefs with whom the Crown signed the treaty
whichchose, animalthe decision which ended segregation
thatpersonne ou chose, relative déterminative seulementthe law that banned redlining
whoseappartenance (« dont le / la / les »)families whose homes were redlined
where / whenlieu / momentthe area where she grew up / the year when the Act was signed

Whose

Whose est suivi directement du nom possédé, sans article : Ruth Bader Ginsburg, whose dissents became famous, served for 27 years. (dont les opinions dissidentes)

Relatives déterminatives et appositives

  • Déterminative (defining) : indispensable pour identifier l'antécédent, sans virgule ; that est possible : The Justices who wrote the opinion were in the majority.
  • Appositive (non-defining) : information supplémentaire, entre virgules ; that est impossible : Thurgood Marshall, who won Brown, joined the Court in 1967.

L'omission du relatif

Dans une déterminative, le relatif complément peut disparaître : the case (that) Marshall won, the woman (who) I met. Le relatif sujet ne peut pas être omis : the man who lives here.

Avec une préposition, l'anglais courant la rejette à la fin : the area (that) she lives in ; l'anglais soutenu dit the area in which she lives.

Attention

« Ce que » se dit what : What the Court decided surprised everyone. Et pour reprendre toute une proposition, on emploie which après une virgule : The proposal was rejected, which disappointed its supporters.

Vouloir que quelqu'un fasse

Le français emploie « que » + subjonctif ; l'anglais emploie verbe + complément + to + BV :

  • The activists want the government to build more social housing. (veulent que le gouvernement construise)
  • Voters expected the Court to protect their rights. (s'attendaient à ce que la Cour protège)
  • I would like you to explain your point of view. (j'aimerais que tu expliques)

Le complément est un pronom complément : She wants them to vote (jamais she wants that they vote).

D'autres verbes suivent ce modèle : ask, tell, allow, encourage, force, help, need, persuade, advise : The law allowed tenants to buy their homes. The judge told the parties to stand up. Négation : not avant to : She asked them not to leave.

Make, let et be made to

make (obliger) et let (laisser) sont suivis de la base verbale sans to : The guards made visitors show their ID. They let us in. Au passif, to réapparaît : Visitors were made to show their ID.

Empêcher, interdire

prevent / stop / bar + sb + from + V-ing : Redlining prevented families from buying homes. They were barred from voting.

Attention

Hope ne suit pas ce modèle : I hope (that) they will win, et non I hope them to win. Avec suggest, on dit I suggest that she (should) apply ou I suggest applying.

chapitres.a_retenir:
• Le redlining (années 1930) a privé des quartiers noirs et immigrés de prêts immobiliers ; le Fair Housing Act (1968) l'a interdit. Au Royaume-Uni, les council houses et les quartiers mixtes visent la mixité sociale.
  • La Cour suprême compte neuf juges nommés à vie par le président et confirmés par le Sénat. Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) a validé la ségrégation ; Brown v. Board of Education (1954) l'a déclarée inconstitutionnelle à l'école. La Cour peut renverser ses précédents (Roe v. Wade en 2022).
  • En Nouvelle-Zélande, des sièges maoris existent depuis 1867 ; en Australie, la Voice to Parliament a été rejetée par référendum en 2023. Ces dispositifs posent la question : intégration ou reconnaissance symbolique ?
  • Passif : be + participe passé ; be porte le temps ; agent introduit par by ; « on » se traduit souvent par un passif (They were given the vote).
  • Relatifs : who (personne), which (chose), that (déterminatives seulement), whose + nom sans article (appartenance), whom (personne complément, soutenu).
  • want / expect / would like / ask + sb + to + BV ; make / let + sb + BV ; prevent / bar sb from V-ing.
